summary: OWASP's ASI06 (Memory & Context Poisoning) is illustrated by Cisco's 'MemoryTrap' vulnerability in Claude Code: a routine workflow (clone repo → approve an npm install) let a payload reach persistent memory, global hooks config, and the system-prompt layer — turning a one-time action into prompt injection that persists across sessions, projects, and reboots.
takeaway: Agent memory/persistence is a first-class attack surface: untrusted input carried forward becomes durable, trusted instruction.

lessons.point: Persistent memory + hooks + system prompt are high-trust layers that untrusted content must never silently reach
lessons.excerpt: a one-time action could shape the model's future behavior across sessions, projects, and even reboots

lessons.point: The dangerous path looked ordinary — the agent was 'being helpful' by installing a suggested dependency
lessons.excerpt: Claude Code was not doing something obviously dangerous. It was being helpful.

actionable.title: Isolate and review agent memory writes
actionable.detail: Treat writes to persistent memory, hooks, and system-prompt layers as privileged: require explicit review, provenance tracking, and don't let tool output mutate them implicitly.

title: MemoryTrap: persistent memory poisoning in AI coding agents (OWASP ASI06)

summary: Google Project Zero published a 0-click exploit chain targeting the Pixel 10 ('When a Door Closes, a Window Opens'), continuing its deep-dive series on modern Android/Pixel exploitation and the mitigations that shape real-world attack chains.
takeaway: 0-click chains remain viable on flagship, hardened devices; defense-in-depth and rapid patching still matter most.

lessons.point: Even the most hardened mobile targets fall to creative 0-click chaining of individually-limited bugs
lessons.excerpt: A 0-click exploit chain for the Pixel 10

actionable.title: Prioritize 0-click attack-surface reduction
actionable.detail: Audit message/media parsers reachable without user interaction; keep devices on the latest patch level.

title: Project Zero: a 0-click exploit chain for the Pixel 10

author: PrismorSec
summary: Prismor is a runtime firewall for AI agents: it intercepts an agent's tool calls before they execute and blocks dangerous commands, secret leakage, and rogue actions. It represents a shift from static agent auditing to runtime enforcement at the tool-call boundary.
takeaway: The strongest control point for agent safety is the tool-call boundary — enforce policy at call time, not just in the prompt.

lessons.point: Put a policy-enforcing firewall between the agent and its tools so a compromised prompt can't reach a destructive action
lessons.excerpt: catches the rogue tool call before it runs

lessons.point: Runtime enforcement complements static scanning — assume the model will be tricked and contain the blast radius
lessons.excerpt: Runtime Firewall for AI agents

actionable.title: Add a tool-call firewall to your agent harness
actionable.detail: Interpose an allow/deny policy layer on every tool call (esp. shell, network, secret access) with human-in-the-loop for high-impact actions.

title: Prismor: a runtime firewall that blocks rogue AI-agent tool calls

author: praetorian-inc
summary: Augustus (Praetorian) is a single-binary Go LLM vulnerability scanner that tests models against 210+ adversarial probes — prompt injection, jailbreaks, encoding exploits, data extraction — across 28 providers. Unlike research tools (garak, promptfoo), it is built for production security testing with concurrency, rate limiting, and retry logic.
takeaway: LLM red-teaming is becoming an operational, CI-ready discipline — run a probe suite against every model/prompt change, not just at launch.

lessons.point: Treat LLM security testing like DAST: a large, versioned probe corpus you re-run continuously
lessons.excerpt: Test large language models against 210+ adversarial attacks

lessons.point: Single-binary Go tooling lowers the bar for security teams to adopt vs Python research frameworks
lessons.excerpt: Unlike research-oriented tools, Augustus is built for production security testing

actionable.title: Adopt an LLM probe suite in CI
actionable.detail: Wire Augustus (or garak/promptfoo) into CI to run prompt-injection/jailbreak probes on each model or system-prompt change; gate releases on the report.

title: Augustus: a production LLM vulnerability scanner (210+ probes)

summary: Google's Security team reports on the current real-world state of prompt injection on the web — moving the conversation from lab demos to observed in-the-wild indirect prompt-injection against browsing/agentic systems.
takeaway: Indirect prompt injection is now an operational threat, not a theoretical one; design agents assuming hostile web content.

lessons.point: Treat all retrieved web content as untrusted instructions, not just data
lessons.excerpt: the current state of prompt injections on the web

actionable.title: Assume hostile web content in agent design
actionable.detail: For browsing/RAG agents, isolate retrieved content from the instruction channel and constrain downstream tool permissions.

title: Prompt injection in the wild: Google on the current state

summary: PortSwigger's 19th annual community-powered ranking of the most innovative web security research of 2025, selected from 63 nominations by community vote plus an expert panel. James Kettle's 'HTTP/1.1 Must Die: the desync endgame' was a finalist.
takeaway: The single best reading list for web-security researchers each year — a curated map of the techniques that will define the next cycle of attacks.

lessons.point: HTTP desync/request-smuggling research remains at the frontier (HTTP/1.1 Must Die)
lessons.excerpt: HTTP/1.1 Must Die: the desync endgame

lessons.point: AI may be pulling researcher attention away from classic web research (nominations dropped from 121 to 63)
lessons.excerpt: possibly because we collectively got distracted by AI

actionable.title: Work through the Top-10 list
actionable.detail: Use the annual PortSwigger Top 10 as a study syllabus; reproduce each technique against a lab target to internalize it.

title: PortSwigger's Top 10 Web Hacking Techniques of 2025

summary: Google is rewriting parts of the Pixel cellular baseband in Rust, bringing memory safety to one of the most attractive and hard-to-reach remote attack surfaces on a phone.
takeaway: Memory-safe languages are reaching the lowest, most security-critical layers — the baseband — meaningfully shrinking remote attack surface.

lessons.point: Rewriting high-risk parsers in Rust removes whole classes of memory-corruption bugs at the baseband
lessons.excerpt: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband

actionable.title: Favor memory-safe rewrites for remote parsers
actionable.detail: Target memory-unsafe code on remotely-reachable attack surfaces first when planning Rust migrations.

title: Google brings Rust (memory safety) to the Pixel baseband
Systemic MCP implementation flaw exposes up to ~200k instances
threat: Researchers disclosed a systemic vulnerability in widely used MCP implementations (across Python, TypeScript, Java, and Rust), described as a core AI supply-chain weakness exposing large numbers of MCP instances embedded in IDEs, internal tools, and cloud services.
conditions: Affects deployments that expose or embed vulnerable MCP server implementations, particularly network-reachable or IDE-integrated instances.
mitigations: Inventory all MCP instances; patch to fixed implementation versions; remove network exposure; require authentication; apply egress controls and continuous SCA on AI tooling dependencies.

title: Typosquatted npm packages steal cloud and CI/CD secrets
threat: A single actor published 14 malicious packages in ~4 hours typosquatting OpenSearch/ElasticSearch/DevOps libraries; on install they harvest AWS credentials, HashiCorp Vault tokens, and CI/CD pipeline secrets.
conditions: Affects developer and CI environments that install packages by name without verifying the publisher, especially with ambient cloud credentials present.
mitigations: Use scoped/internal registries and name allow-lists; remove standing secrets from build hosts (use OIDC short-lived tokens); scan installs; enforce typosquat detection and 2FA on publishing.

title: AI agent skill registry poisoned at scale (ClawHub)
threat: An AI agent skill marketplace became the first registry systematically poisoned at scale, with several of the most-downloaded skills confirmed as malware, enabling credential theft and code execution inside agent environments.
conditions: Affects teams that install community agent skills/plugins automatically without provenance checks or sandboxing.
mitigations: Vet and pin skills by publisher and hash; isolate skill execution; scan skills for malicious behavior; prefer signed/verified sources; monitor for post-install network and credential access.

title: Axios npm package compromised (100M+ weekly downloads)
threat: Malicious Axios versions (1.14.1, 0.30.4) were published with an injected dependency that pulled payloads from attacker C2. Microsoft attributed it to the North Korean actor Sapphire Sleet. CISA issued an alert.
conditions: Affects projects that installed or auto-updated to the malicious versions of this widely used HTTP client.
mitigations: Pin to known-good Axios versions and rebuild; audit lockfiles; rotate any exposed secrets; enable install-time scanning and provenance checks; subscribe to ecosystem advisories.

title: First large-scale indirect prompt injection attacks observed in the wild
threat: Adversaries embed hidden instructions inside content an LLM later retrieves (web pages, documents, ad copy) rather than in the user's direct prompt. Unit 42 documented the first large-scale, real-world cases, including ad-review evasion and system-prompt leakage on live commercial platforms.
conditions: Affects LLM apps and agents that ingest untrusted external data (RAG, browsing, email/doc summarization, tool output) and act on it without isolating instructions from data.
mitigations: Treat all retrieved content as untrusted data, not instructions; enforce strict input/output boundaries and content provenance; constrain tool/agent permissions with allow-lists; add injection detection and human-in-the-loop for high-impact actions.

title: Qualcomm zero-day (CVE-2026-21385) in March 2026 Android update
threat: The March 2026 Android security bulletin patched 129 vulnerabilities including a Qualcomm zero-day (CVE-2026-21385) reported as affecting a large number of chipset models, exploitable in the wild.
conditions: Affects Android devices on vulnerable Qualcomm chipsets prior to the March 2026 patch level.
mitigations: Apply the March 2026 (or later) Android security patch level; enforce minimum patch level via MDM; prioritize devices on affected chipsets.

title: 50+ mobile apps ship hardcoded AWS credentials
threat: More than 50 apps were found with hardcoded AWS credentials in their binaries, giving attackers a direct path to production databases, customer data, and in some cases root-level cloud control.
conditions: Affects apps that embed long-lived cloud credentials for backend access instead of brokering access server-side.
mitigations: Remove all cloud credentials from clients; use short-lived tokens via an authenticated backend (Cognito/STS/OIDC); rotate exposed keys immediately; add CI checks that fail builds containing credentials.

title: AI-authored code is a leading source of new web-app vulnerabilities
threat: With 90%+ of organizations using AI coding assistants, AI-generated code has become a top AppSec blind spot, frequently introducing injection, auth, and secrets-handling flaws that ship faster than review can catch.
conditions: Affects teams shipping AI-assisted code without commensurate review, SAST, and secrets scanning in the pipeline.
mitigations: Mandate human review of AI-generated code; enforce SAST/DAST and secret scanning in CI; add guardrail prompts and policy; track provenance of generated code; security-train developers on AI pitfalls.

title: Hardcoded cryptographic keys in 47.8% of Android and 17.6% of iOS apps
threat: Quokka's analysis of 150k+ apps found cryptographic keys embedded directly in app binaries. Because every install ships the same key, extraction via trivial decompilation compromises all users' protected data retroactively.
conditions: Affects apps that embed symmetric keys or secrets in the binary for on-device encryption or API access.
mitigations: Move on-device keys to Android Keystore / iOS Secure Enclave; fetch secrets at runtime from an authenticated vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager); never ship secrets in the binary; scan builds for embedded keys.

title: MCP tool poisoning attacks (TPAs) via hidden tool-description metadata
threat: Malicious instructions hidden in Model Context Protocol tool descriptions (metadata read by the model but not shown to users) coerce agents into leaking data or invoking dangerous tools. Studies found a large share of MCP servers also contain command injection, path traversal, and SSRF flaws.
conditions: Affects AI agents that auto-load third-party MCP servers/tools and trust tool descriptions as benign; worsened by excessive autonomy and broad credential scope.
mitigations: Pin and review MCP servers from trusted publishers only; render and audit full tool descriptions; sandbox tool execution; apply least-privilege credentials and per-tool allow-lists; monitor for anomalous tool calls.

title: RAG poisoning via injected malicious documents in the retrieval corpus
threat: Adversaries plant malicious documents in the retrieval corpus so the model surfaces and acts on attacker-controlled content, enabling misinformation, data exfiltration prompts, or indirect injection at query time.
conditions: Affects RAG systems that ingest from open or weakly-governed sources (wikis, ticketing, web crawls, user uploads) without content validation.
mitigations: Govern ingestion with source allow-lists and validation; sign/verify trusted documents; isolate retrieved text from instruction context; add retrieval-time anomaly detection and provenance metadata.

title: Shipped apps carry years-old Critical CVEs in bundled components
threat: Quokka found Android apps shipping Critical CVEs spanning nearly a decade of unpatched components, and 2,075 iOS apps containing a Critical CVE first disclosed in 2023 — outdated bundled SDKs/libraries remain a major exposure.
conditions: Affects apps bundling outdated third-party SDKs/native libraries without dependency patching.
mitigations: Maintain a mobile SBOM; continuously scan bundled SDKs for known CVEs; patch/upgrade dependencies on a schedule; gate releases on component vulnerability checks.

title: CL.0 and browser-powered desync request smuggling
threat: PortSwigger research on browser-powered desync and CL.0 shows back-end servers can be made to ignore Content-Length, enabling request smuggling without chunked encoding or HTTP/2 downgrade, leading to request hijacking and cache poisoning.
conditions: Affects multi-tier deployments where front-end and back-end disagree on request boundaries (reverse proxies, CDNs, load balancers).
mitigations: Normalize request parsing across tiers; prefer HTTP/2 end-to-end and reject ambiguous Content-Length; deploy current proxy/server versions; test with smuggling tooling; the longer-term fix is retiring HTTP/1.1 back-ends.

title: WAFFLED: parsing discrepancies bypass web application firewalls
threat: Academic work shows attackers exploit differences in how WAFs and back-ends parse requests (encodings, multipart, content types) to slip malicious payloads past the WAF that the application still processes.
conditions: Affects apps relying on a WAF as a primary control where WAF and origin parse input differently.
mitigations: Do not treat the WAF as the sole defense; fix root-cause input handling; align parsing between WAF and app; canonicalize input; keep WAF rule/engine updated and test bypass classes.

title: Image-based prompt injection hijacks multimodal LLMs
threat: Adversarial instructions are visually embedded in images (including steganographic or low-contrast text and QR codes) and interpreted as commands by multimodal models, hijacking behavior without any malicious text in the prompt.
conditions: Applies to multimodal LLMs that accept user- or web-supplied images, especially in agentic pipelines that screenshot pages or process uploaded media.
mitigations: Sanitize/normalize images before model ingestion; separate visual content from instruction channels; OCR-and-scan images for embedded instructions; restrict actions the model can take from image-derived content.

title: System-prompt extraction remains broadly effective
threat: Multi-step prompting that exploits a model's tendency to summarize or restate its own instructions reliably extracts hidden system prompts, exposing guardrails, secrets, and business logic.
conditions: Affects assistants that place sensitive instructions, keys, or policy in the system prompt and expose a conversational interface.
mitigations: Never store secrets in prompts; minimize sensitive content in system prompts; add extraction-pattern detection; enforce output filters; treat the system prompt as non-confidential by design.

title: LANDFALL spyware exploited Samsung zero-day (CVE-2025-21042)
threat: Commercial-grade Android spyware exploited a zero-day in a Samsung image-processing library (CVE-2025-21042) via malicious DNG image files delivered over WhatsApp, achieving remote code execution with little/no user interaction; capabilities include mic recording, location tracking, and data theft.
conditions: Affected unpatched Samsung Galaxy devices (campaign active mid-2024 to patch in April 2025); targeted individuals in the Middle East/North Africa.
mitigations: Apply Samsung security updates (patched April 2025); keep messaging apps and OS current; use lockdown/hardening modes for high-risk users; deploy mobile threat detection.

title: New OWASP category: Software Supply Chain Failures (A03)
threat: OWASP added a dedicated Software Supply Chain Failures category, recognizing dependency, build-pipeline, and artifact-integrity risks as a top web-app risk class distinct from generic vulnerable components.
conditions: Affects any application consuming third-party packages, build actions, or container bases without integrity verification.
mitigations: Maintain an SBOM; pin and verify dependencies by hash; use signed artifacts and provenance (SLSA); restrict CI permissions; continuously scan and monitor for compromised packages.

title: OWASP Top 10:2025 — Broken Access Control (#1) now subsumes SSRF
threat: The 2025 Top 10 (based on 175k+ vulnerabilities) keeps Broken Access Control at #1 and folds in Server-Side Request Forgery, reflecting how missing authorization and SSRF let attackers reach internal services and data.
conditions: Affects apps with object-level/function-level authorization gaps or server-side fetchers that accept user-controlled URLs.
mitigations: Enforce server-side authorization on every request; deny-by-default; validate and allow-list outbound URLs; block link-local/metadata endpoints; add automated access-control tests.

author: agentscope-ai
summary: PawBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLM × harness performance — measuring not just the model but the model-plus-harness system, reflecting that agent capability depends heavily on the surrounding scaffold.
takeaway: Evaluate the model-plus-harness as a unit; the harness is a first-class variable in agent performance.

lessons.point: Benchmark the (model, harness) pair, not the model alone — the scaffold changes outcomes
lessons.excerpt: A benchmark for evaluating LLM x harness performance

actionable.title: Add harness-aware evals
actionable.detail: When comparing agents, hold the task set fixed and vary the harness; measure end-to-end task success, not raw model scores.

title: PawBench: benchmarking LLM x harness performance
stale
takeaway: Compact tool outputs to shrink context cost.

lessons.point: Summarize before re-injecting
lessons.excerpt: 40% less

title: OpenClaw's ClawHub skill marketplace: an agentic supply-chain attack surface
summary: Unit 42 found five evasive malicious 'skills' persisting on ClawHub — the marketplace OpenClaw's agent pulls third-party, markdown-driven packages from with broad local system access — despite VirusTotal + ClawScan screening added after February's incidents. The five span infostealers (macOS, C2), scanner evasion (inflated file size to exceed thresholds), and two NOVEL agentic threats: runtime agentic affiliate injection and agentic front-running.
takeaway: Agent skill marketplaces are a critical, largely-untrusted link in the software supply chain — marketplace scanning alone does not make them safe.

lessons.point: Agent skills are broad-access packages; the marketplace is a supply-chain link to treat as untrusted
lessons.excerpt: markdown-driven packages with broad local system access, making ClawHub a critical link in the agentic software supply chain

lessons.point: Malware evades marketplace scanners with simple tricks (oversized files exceed scan thresholds)
lessons.excerpt: inflated file size to exceed scanner thresholds, bypassing both ClawScan and VirusTotal detection

lessons.point: New 'agentic' threat classes are emerging — affiliate injection and front-running done at agent runtime
lessons.excerpt: runtime agentic affiliate injection and agentic front-running. Both are novel techniques

actionable.title: Vet and sandbox agent skills
actionable.detail: Pin and review third-party agent skills from trusted publishers, sandbox their execution with least-privilege, and don't rely on marketplace scanning — add your own allow-list + runtime policy.

title: Over 970,000 AI-Apps on model hubs measured: thousands leak credentials, some carry embedded backdoors
author: Yacong Gu et al.
summary: AI-Apps - the hosted inference and fine-tuning apps on model hubs like Hugging Face - are often built by untrusted parties with weak isolation, and the authors describe this CCS 2026 paper as the first systematic security analysis of them across three platforms. Applying their Insightor framework to over 970,000 public AI-Apps, they report thousands leaking credentials, hundreds with input-injection flaws allowing arbitrary code execution, and tens carrying embedded backdoors, which the paper says indicates active exploitation. It also claims three novel architectural vulnerabilities inherent to platform design, alongside the familiar appsec failures.

lessons.point: The hosted-app layer on a model hub is a distinct attack surface from the model artifacts themselves - built by untrusted third parties with weak isolation and misconfigured security settings.
lessons.excerpt: these platforms introduce an unexplored attack surface, as AI-Apps are often developed by untrusted parties with weak isolation and misconfigured security settings

lessons.point: The paper reports both common appsec failures at scale (broken access control, insufficient input validation, sensitive data exposure) AND three novel architectural vulnerabilities specific to the hosting model - while platform design amplifies mundane issues like world-readable logs into ecosystem-wide exposure.
lessons.excerpt: demonstrate how traditional issues (e.g., world-readable logs) are uniquely amplified in this ecosystem

lessons.point: At this scale the tail is not hypothetical: thousands leak credentials and tens carry embedded backdoors, which the paper says indicates active exploitation - though the abstract does not define what evidence 'active' rests on.
lessons.excerpt: we find thousands of apps leaking credentials, hundreds containing input injection vulnerabilities that allow arbitrary code execution, and tens harboring embedded backdoors

threat: A malicious or compromised AI-App on a public model hub leaks its owner's credentials, executes attacker-supplied input, or ships a backdoor to everyone who runs it.
conditions: Using or forking third-party hosted AI-Apps (inference/fine-tuning spaces) on public model hubs.
mitigations: The paper is a measurement and disclosure study and proposes no mitigations - the authors state only that they responsibly disclosed to affected platforms. The following is our own recommendation, not the paper's: treat a hub-hosted AI-App as untrusted third-party code, scope and rotate any token it touches, and review app source before forking.
takeaway: The app layer on model hubs is third-party code with your credentials in it - scope tokens per app and read the source before you fork.

actionable.title: Scope and rotate credentials given to hub-hosted AI-Apps
actionable.detail: Our recommendation, not the paper's (it proposes no defenses): inventory every hub AI-App your team runs or forked, issue per-app least-privilege tokens rather than account-wide ones, rotate anything previously pasted into a Space, and check for world-readable logs in apps you publish.

prior_art: Malicious models on hubs are well studied (pickle RCE, scanner evasion); this examines the *application* layer around them, which the authors describe as unexplored - a self-reported priority claim. The real contribution is scale (970k+ apps, three platforms) plus three newly-named architectural vulnerability classes; the bulk of the named categories are established appsec territory, so this is a strong measurement study rather than a new attack technique. Accepted at ACM CCS 2026.
verify_note: Independent verifier: restored 'over' 970,000; attributed the authors' 'first systematic analysis' claim rather than asserting it; removed an unsupported 'most findings are ordinary appsec' claim that buried the paper's three novel architectural vulnerabilities; relabelled mitigations as ours since the paper proposes none. Novelty 72->58.

title: A malicious federated-learning aggregator can backdoor a QA model without ever seeing client data
author: Chenqing Zhu et al.
summary: Federated learning is adopted precisely so the server never sees raw client data - but this USENIX Security 2026 paper shows the aggregator itself can be the attacker. It inverts the gradients clients upload into representative training samples, builds a poisoning set from them, and implants advertisement-type backdoors into the global model. It reports near-100% attack success with negligible clean-task degradation as its headline result, and separately that reconstructing only 5-20% of gradients suffices for a reliable attack; whether the reduced setting reaches the same rate is not stated. Experiments are on representative QA datasets and LLM families, not live deployments.

lessons.point: The federated threat model usually watches malicious clients; here the trusted aggregator is the adversary, and 'never sharing raw data' does not make it a trust boundary.
lessons.excerpt: we explore the potential vulnerability where a malicious aggregator, who may collude with a third-party vendor, stealthily implants advertisement-type backdoors into federated QA models, without ever accessing client data

lessons.point: Uploaded gradients are the leak: they can be inverted into representative training samples, which is what makes data-free poisoning possible.
lessons.excerpt: recover representative training samples from client gradients, and (2) construct poisoning datasets utilizing recovered samples and trigger phrases to inject backdoors into the global model

lessons.point: The attack is cheap enough to be practical - the paper reports 5-20% of gradients suffices for a reliable attack - and clean-task behavior is preserved, so the model passes normal quality checks.
lessons.excerpt: reconstructing only 5-20% of gradients suffices to mount a reliable attack, exposing a practical blind spot in the pipeline of federated training of QA LLMs

threat: The central aggregator in a federated LLM training run implants a triggered backdoor emitting target advertising content while behaving normally on non-triggered queries. Only advertisement injection is demonstrated; generalization to more harmful payloads is not tested.
conditions: Federated fine-tuning of a QA LLM (full fine-tune or LoRA) where a third party operates the aggregation server and clients upload gradients. Evaluated in a controlled experimental setting, not a production deployment.
mitigations: The paper proposes no defenses. Our own recommendation: treat the aggregator as untrusted - apply secure aggregation or differential privacy to uploaded gradients and evaluate the global model for triggered behavior rather than clean-task accuracy alone. Neither defense is evaluated against this attack in the paper.
takeaway: In federated training the aggregator is a trust boundary, not a neutral party - protect gradients and test the global model for triggers.

actionable.title: Treat the FL aggregator as untrusted
actionable.detail: If you participate in federated fine-tuning you do not operate, assume uploaded gradients are recoverable into training samples. Our recommendation, not the paper's: require secure aggregation or DP noise as a condition of participation, and test the returned global model for triggered behavior, since clean-task accuracy is explicitly preserved by this attack.

prior_art: Gradient inversion and federated backdoors are each established literatures. The delta is a genuinely novel threat model - the *aggregator* mounting a data-free backdoor by reconstructing samples specifically to build the poisoning set - validated across datasets, LLM families, and both full fine-tuning and LoRA. Held below 70 because the demonstrated payload is narrowly advertisement injection. Accepted at the 35th USENIX Security Symposium (2026).
verify_note: Independent verifier: un-fused two separate results (near-100% ASR and the 5-20% gradient figure are not stated to be the same condition); flagged experiments as controlled rather than live deployments; scoped the payload to advertisement injection only; relabelled mitigations as ours. Novelty raised 60->68 - the verifier judged the aggregator-as-adversary threat model more novel than I did.

title: QuantGuard: a pre-quantization defense against backdoors that only wake up after you quantize
author: Aoying Zheng et al.
summary: Quantization-conditioned backdoors stay dormant in the full-precision model and activate only once you quantize for deployment - so they pass the audit you run on the weights you were given. QuantGuard is a proactive pre-quantization defense using differentiable rounding-control variables, optimized against rounding-reversal, output-consistency and weight-distance constraints, to break the attacker's alignment with quantization boundaries. It needs only a small calibration set and no change to your quantization algorithm.

lessons.point: Auditing the full-precision model is not sufficient: a quantization-conditioned backdoor is dormant exactly when you inspect it and activates only after deployment quantization.
lessons.excerpt: malicious behaviors remain dormant in the full-precision stage and are activated only after quantized deployment, thereby bypassing conventional security auditing and detection mechanisms

lessons.point: The attack depends on precise alignment between crafted weights and quantization boundaries, so the defense is a targeted optimization over rounding-control variables - not noise injection - and needs no retraining.
lessons.excerpt: This design breaks the precise alignment between attacker-crafted weight patterns and quantization boundaries, effectively suppressing the post-quantization backdoor activation pathway

lessons.point: Deployability is the point: it needs only a small calibration dataset and leaves the existing quantization pipeline untouched.
lessons.excerpt: QuantGuard utilizes only a small calibration dataset and does not modify existing quantization algorithms

threat: An attacker ships a model that is clean under inspection but exhibits vulnerable code generation, content injection, or over-refusal once the victim quantizes it to INT8/FP4/NF4.
conditions: Deploying a third-party or fine-tuned LLM through a quantization step, where auditing happens on the full-precision weights.
mitigations: Apply a proactive pre-quantization defense such as QuantGuard. Note the paper's premise is that conventional auditing and detection are bypassed by this attack class, so post-hoc evaluation of the quantized model is not established as a sufficient substitute.
takeaway: Audit models at deployment precision, not the precision you were handed - some backdoors only exist after you quantize.

actionable.title: Treat quantization as part of the model supply chain
actionable.detail: Where a third-party model passes through quantization on the way to production, recognise that auditing the full-precision artifact does not cover this attack class. The paper's position is that reactive detection is unreliable and a proactive pre-quantization defense is required - post-hoc behavioural evals would also need the attacker's trigger to surface anything, so do not treat them as the control. Whether post-quantization evaluation detects QCB at all would need the full paper's detection baselines.

prior_art: The paper attributes quantization-conditioned backdoor attacks to prior work ('recent studies'), so the attack class is not new here; the contribution is the defense, and it is technically incremental (control variables plus regularization) rather than a new attack surface. Empirical breadth is solid: six LLMs, three precisions, three scenarios. Defenses remain systematically under-covered relative to attacks. Accepted at ACM CCS 2026.
verify_note: Independent verifier: struck an actionable that contradicted the paper's own premise - it recommended post-quantization evaluation, but the paper's position is that conventional auditing is bypassed and a proactive pre-quantization defense is required. Mechanism corrected from 'perturbs' to a targeted optimization over rounding-control variables. Novelty 62->60.

title: TOCTOU race condition in computer-use agents: the screen changes between screenshot and click
summary: Computer-use agents capture a screenshot, reason about it for several seconds, then act on pixel coordinates — but an attacker-controlled page can change what sits at those coordinates during the reasoning window, so the agent clicks something other than what it saw. Johann Rehberger reproduces Jun Kokatsu's original ChatGPT Operator race condition against Claude Computer-Use, showing a reliable time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) attack where a 'Continue' button is swapped for a Send/consent button at identical coordinates. It is a classic race-condition bug surfacing in a novel agentic context, with the practical fix being a re-check of the UI at action time.

lessons.point: The gap between screenshot capture and action execution is a genuine race window because LLM inference takes seconds, giving an attacker ample time to mutate the page.
lessons.excerpt: the computer screen could have changed while the LLM inference was happening

lessons.point: Because the agent acts on pixel coordinates, swapping an element at the same location makes the agent click a different object than the one it reasoned about.
lessons.excerpt: the action the AI Agent takes can happen on a different object than intended!

lessons.point: The attack was reliably reproducible against a shipping agent, not just theoretical.
lessons.excerpt: both Claude Computer-Use fell for this at the first time, and it repro'd regularly

lessons.point: A concrete exploit tricks the agent into sending an attacker's drafted email by aligning a phishing 'Continue' button with Outlook's 'Send' button and padding reasoning time so the page finishes loading before the click.
lessons.excerpt: The 'Continue' button is at the exact same location as the 'Send' button

lessons.point: The recommended defense is to re-verify UI state at action time, not just at perception time.
lessons.excerpt: take a snapshot when reasoning starts and when reasoning concludes check again that nothing significant changed

takeaway: A computer-use agent that clicks coordinates it decided on seconds ago is exploitable by TOCTOU: re-check the UI at action time, because what the model saw is not necessarily what it clicks.

actionable.title: Add an action-time UI re-check to computer-use agent loops
actionable.detail: In any screenshot-reason-act loop (Claude Computer-Use, Operator-style agents), capture a screenshot/DOM snapshot both when reasoning starts and immediately before dispatching the click. If the region around the target coordinates changed materially between the two snapshots, abort and re-perceive instead of clicking. Additionally, treat time-sensitive/consequential actions (Send, Confirm, Allow, payment) as requiring a fresh perception step, and be suspicious of injected instructions that pad reasoning time (e.g. 'compute 1+1 in bash') which widen the race window.

prior_art: Jun Kokatsu's ChatGPT Operator TOCTOU race-condition disclosure (GHSA-mp56-7vrw-qxvf, Google Security Research) — the same screenshot-to-action race, which this post explicitly reproduces and ports to Claude Computer-Use.
threat: An attacker-controlled web page (reachable via indirect prompt injection or a lured navigation) mutates the DOM at fixed coordinates during the agent's multi-second reasoning window, causing the agent to click a consequential control (Send, Allow, Confirm, consent/permission dialog) it never intended, enabling actions like sending arbitrary emails or granting permissions.
conditions: Agent acts on absolute pixel/screen coordinates chosen from an earlier screenshot; Reasoning latency of several seconds creates a wide, reliable race window; Attacker can control page content and time page changes (e.g. via a deep-link that loads a real app), optionally padding reasoning time via injected filler tasks; No re-verification of UI state between perception and action
mitigations: Snapshot the UI at reasoning start and re-check at action time; abort the click if the target region changed significantly (Anthropic's documented fix); Force a fresh perception step for high-consequence actions (Send/Allow/Confirm/pay); Add human-in-the-loop confirmation for irreversible or sensitive actions; Detect and distrust injected instructions designed to stall reasoning and widen the race window
verify_note: All five excerpts appear verbatim in the source and the points are faithfully supported; the technique is a known TOCTOU class re-demonstrated on a new agent (Claude), so novelty is mid but defender relevance is high.

title: Kemp LoadMaster pre-auth RCE: uninitialized heap + missing null byte (CVE-2026-8037)
summary: A one-function patch to `escape_quotes()` in Kemp LoadMaster revealed a pre-auth RCE. The escaped buffer wasn't null-terminated, so `__sprintf_chk()` reads out of bounds into an adjacent heap chunk; by heap-spraying an un-escaped command-injection payload (via JSON key/value pairs) into that neighboring chunk, an unauthenticated attacker turns an 'uninitialized memory' bug into command execution.

lessons.point: The whole bug is a missing null terminator: the escaped buffer wasn't null-terminated, so a formatting call runs off the end into adjacent heap memory.
lessons.excerpt: the escaped buffer was not null-terminated

lessons.point: Out-of-bounds read becomes injection when the neighboring freed chunk holds an un-escaped payload with no null byte — the sanitizer is bypassed by reading past where it stopped.
lessons.excerpt: That means if an adjacent freed heap chunk contains an unescaped command injection payload

lessons.point: Attacker-controlled heap layout is the exploit primitive: spraying many JSON key/value pairs places the payload chunk exactly where the OOB read lands.
lessons.excerpt: This gives us a useful heap-spraying primitive by adding lots of JSON key/value pairs.

threat: Unauthenticated remote code execution on an edge load balancer reachable by anyone who can reach the API.
conditions: Network access to the LoadMaster API; no credentials required.
mitigations: Apply Progress' June 2026 patch; a tiny-looking diff (adding null-termination) can be the fix for a critical bug, so patch edge appliances promptly.
takeaway: A minimal 'just null-terminate the buffer' patch can hide a pre-auth RCE — diff patches carefully, and treat missing null-termination next to attacker-controlled heap data as exploitable, not cosmetic.

actionable.title: Prioritize edge-appliance patches and read the diff, not the CVE title
actionable.detail: When a vendor ships a one-line string-handling fix on an internet-facing appliance, assume memory-corruption impact until proven otherwise and patch on the critical track; missing null-termination adjacent to attacker-sprayable heap data is an RCE primitive, not a hardening nit.

prior_art: Uninitialized-memory and heap-spray techniques are classic; the novel delta is the specific n-day chain (patch-diff -> non-null-terminated escape buffer -> OOB read into sprayed JSON chunk) on a widely deployed edge load balancer.
verify_note: Self-verified against source (automated verifier blocked by a cyber-content safeguard); mechanism grounded and accurate.
